title: Your Own Web Server
summary: Start a real web server on your computer, talk to it with curl and stop it again.
intro:
Every website lives on a server: a computer program that waits for requests and sends back pages.
Today you will start your very own web server, right here on your computer!
It is safe: only your own computer can reach it, and it works without internet.
outro: You ran a real web server, asked it for pages, read its log and stopped it. That is exactly how the web works, just on a much bigger scale. Awesome job!

setup.content:
# Terminal Academy: hide curl's progress bar (a normal terminal does not show it either), but still show errors.
silent
show-error

steps.instruction: Go into the folder site. It has the files of your website.
steps.explain: The server will share the files of the folder it starts in. So it's important to be in the right place.

steps.instruction: Start a web server on port 8765, only for this computer, in the background. Save its messages in server.log.
hints: Python has a small web server built in: python3 -m http.server. Don't forget the & at the end, or the server blocks your terminal.
> server.log 2>&1 sends all its messages into the file server.log.
steps.explain: A server is a program that waits for requests on a port. --bind 127.0.0.1 means only your own computer can reach it. If cat server.log ever shows 'Address already in use', another program has that port: use 8766 instead (also in the next steps).

steps.instruction: Ask your server for the file hello.txt.
hints: A URL is: http:// + address + : + port + /file
steps.explain: You are the client, Python is the server. The client asks, the server answers. That's how the whole web works! http://localhost:8765/hello.txt works too.

steps.instruction: Ask only for the headers of the main page (the URL that ends with just /).
hints: curl -I asks only for the 'head' of the answer, not the page itself.
steps.explain: 200 OK means 'all good, here it is'. The headers also tell the type of the content (text/html) and its size. If you type the same URL in your browser, you see your page!

steps.instruction: Ask for a page that does not exist, like /nope.html.
hints: Same as before, but with a different file name.
steps.explain: 404 Not Found: you have seen this on websites. Now you know where it comes from: the server looked for the file and didn't find it.

steps.instruction: Servers write down every request. Read your server's log file, server.log.
hints: It's a normal text file. Which command shows a file?
steps.explain: Each line is one request: who asked (127.0.0.1), when, what (GET /hello.txt) and the answer code (200 or 404). Real websites keep logs like this too.

steps.instruction: Time to clean up. Find the PID of the server and stop it with kill.
hints: ps aux | grep http.server shows the server. The PID is in the second column. Then: kill PID
pgrep -f "http.server 8765" prints just the PID of your server. You can put it right into kill with $( ).
steps.explain: Always stop servers you don't need anymore. (Terminal Academy also stops them when you leave a lesson, but your real terminal won't!)

steps.instruction: Prove it: ask the server for hello.txt one more time.
hints: Use the same curl command as in step 3. You can press the Up arrow to find it.
steps.explain: Nobody answers anymore: 'Failed to connect' means no program is waiting on that port. Your server is really gone.
